item.title: Gemini 4 Argon
item.description:
Source: deepmind.google

See also: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50074869

Top Comment:

We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon in 100 unsaturated, competitive and cooperative coding environments. It's roughly in between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 in our testing, so it's maybe 2 months behind the frontier.

Google's major releases have usually done pretty well on our benchmarks because they're good at hard problems and open-ended decision making (with a well specified prompt), which obviously doesn't always translate to user experience. In particular, older Google models struggled to work efficiently in a harness. They seem to have solved that with Argon.

We did see a new problem which I hope they can fix. This is the first near-frontier model we've caught in infinite reasoning loops in a long time. We also saw a few examples of it failing to properly delineate reasoning blocks, so it has a higher failure rate than its competitors.

My overall impression is that Argon is a near-frontier model for engineering design, code analysis, and chat. It definitely has the intelligence to be a competitive coding assistant product, but a good coding assistant needs to be polished, so I hope they can clean up the CoT bugs.

Data at https://gertlabs.com/rankings

item.title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
item.description:
Source: www.bleepingcomputer.com

https://www.heise.de/en/news/Crypto-thieves-sell-hardware-wa...

https://crypto.news/ledger-confirms-hidden-chip-in-crypto-wa...

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8JnHdr30v4g

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nf4FEFlgv3Q

https://www.tibane.net/research/ledger-nano-x-implant

Top Comment:

No matter whether you like or hate or don't care about cryptocurrencies, this is incredible stuff...

Now basically: every single attack that's been described as "theoretical" or "far-fetched" or "only existing in the mind of a paranoid person" did actually happen.

We're talking here about a tiny eSIM implant and a little CPU doing OCR on the fonts appearing on the hardware wallet's screen to read the secrets during set up. So the secure element ain't tampered with.

Not long ago the Coldcard hardware wallet had an issue where it'd fallback to a 32-bit only RNG that could be cracked and so many people got their coins stolen.

Now it's Ledger that sees tampered devices all around the world (in Asia for sure but now there are reports about reseller in the EU selling backdoored/eSIM'ed devices).

For people who own Bitcoin at this point one of the only thing kinda sensible to do is to use multisig schemes, like 2-of-2 or 3-of-3 multisig, where your split the secret over two or three different hardware wallet brands (meaning being able to sign a 2-of-2 wallets requires hardware wallets from two different vendors).

When Ledger hardware wallets came out and people said that seed (the list of words) could be intercepted and relayed by a channel bypassing the computer (here by using an eSIM), people would post explaining that people were nuts if they thought such an attack could be pulled off.

Yet here we are.

And Ledger is responsible for very poor security practices: for example it's impossible to use a Ledger hardware wallet in a fully airgapped/offline way. For you're forced to not only upgrade the firmware but also install the Bitcoin "ledger app" (or whatever that is called) after you entered your seed into the device.

Which is complete and total amateur hour.

In addition to that Ledger offers a service to "backup your seed": what could possibly go wrong with that uh?

I'm betting that we'll soon hear about hardware wallets getting drained due to the seed being exfiltrated through "randomness" in how transactions are built/signed (aka "kleptography").

And it's not just representative about people in the cryptocurrencies ecosystem: people simply don't understand computer security and don't understand the potential attacks nor the length at which attackers are willing to go to steal data/funds/ruin other people's lives.

At this point we've heard about chips' plans being modified before the chips are even built (only to lower the entropy of RNGs) [unrelated to cryptocurrencies btw], a worldwide backdoor attempt in SSH, eSIM sending secrets from hardware wallets with tiny attack surfaces.

You're not anywhere near paranoid enough.

item.description:

I don't know enough to argue about whether passkeys are a trap or not, but I do know as a user that they appear to be a confusing mess.

When a website prompts me to set up a passkey, depending on the device I happen to be using at the time it could end up going to Google password manager, Samsung password manager, iCloud Keychain, or Windows somethingorother.

What happens when I go to the same site on a different platform? What if I can't use cross-device authentication because I'm on a locked-down work machine or one that simply doesn't have bluetooth? What if I want to consolidate them all in one platform just for the sake of being organised? What if I lose or simply don't have the device with a certain passkey near me?

I don't have the time or patience to work out any of that, which might absolutely be a 'me' problem, but TOTPs are pretty sodding frictionless in comparison. Scan QR in my chosen manager; type number into website; done. Why are passkeys better?

item.title: Recreational Programming
item.description:
Source: www.cphiri.dev

Top Comment:

A harsh reality that I didn't come to terms with until I was in my late 30s is that many things I enjoy doing still cost spoons to do. Which means I can also burn myself out doing things I enjoy. Programming is one of those things, so programming in my free time was still burning me out even though I found it rewarding.

My mental health improved quite a bit when I realized I needed to identify and prioritize more restorative forms of play. That did mean allowing my childhood passion to become just a day job. But that's OK. I honestly wish I had let it happen sooner. What got me to where I am now won't necessarily get me to where I want to go next.

If that's not how things work for you and programming for fun is genuinely restorative, great. I just wanted to put my own experience out there because tech's hustle culture can make it hard to realize that advice like this isn't for everybody. Especially for those of us who might have a touch of alexithymia. Which seems to be pretty common among professional programmers.

item.title: Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing.

- pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW index has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that).

- pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out.

- pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.

item.title: Why do LLM pelicans look like this?
item.description:
Source: arcfu.com

Top Comment:

I'm not clear on what the claim is here.

The article faults LLMs for not being more creative (riding in the city in the rain, in East Asia, in outer space, etc.). But, if prompted, "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle," with no additional details or specification, then I would _expect_ something generic: a side view, nondescript terrain or perhaps terrain associated with a pelican (i.e., beach), little clothing (because birds don't wear clothes) with the possible exception of something strongly associated with bicyclists (a helmet).

The article talks about "the LLM diversity collapse problem," which makes it sound like LLMs are getting less diverse over time, but the linked benchmarks suggest that newer, more capable models are _more_ creative.

Out of curiosity, I tried a couple of prompt variations in Opus 5.5. "Be creative" did a beach scene but added fish to the bike basket and a lighthouse in the background - not too creative. "Pick a unique and creative variation of this concept" resulted in a "midnight circus act" of a pelican riding a penny-farthing on a tightrope while balancing a fishing pole with fish (and, this time, two lighthouses - the tightrope is implausibly strung between them).
